# Brand Identity Models: Aaker and Kapferer’s Frameworks

Last updated on:

November 27, 2025

What makes a brand truly recognizable – not just its logo, but its entire character? That’s the question two of the world’s leading brand theorists set out to answer. David Aaker, Professor Emeritus at UC Berkeley’s Haas School of Business, and Jean-Noël Kapferer, professor of marketing strategy at HEC Paris, each developed frameworks that go far beyond visual design. Their models – Aaker’s Brand Identity System and Kapferer’s Brand Identity Prism – remain the most widely used tools for building deep, durable brand identities. Understanding both is essential for anyone serious about brand strategy.

## David Aaker’s brand identity model 🔗

Introduced in his 1996 book Building Strong Brands, Aaker’s model was a direct challenge to the short-sighted branding practices of its time. Advertising agencies were defining brands through a single phrase or campaign concept. Aaker argued that this produced shallow identities – ones that were easy to copy and quick to fade. His model proposed something richer: a structured system of 8-12 identity elements organized around a core identity (the brand’s timeless essence) and an extended identity (supporting elements that add texture and detail).

The core insight is that a brand vision should attempt to go beyond functional benefits to consider organizational values, higher purpose, brand personality, and emotional, social, and self-expressive benefits. To make sure no dimension is overlooked, Aaker asks strategists to examine the brand through four distinct perspectives.

### Deep dive: the four perspectives of Aaker’s model 🔗

### Brand as a product 🔗

This is usually the starting point for most brands. The product perspective covers scope, attributes, quality and value, uses, users, and country or region of origin. It asks: what does this brand make, and what functional or emotional benefit does it deliver? Aaker’s goal here is not simply to trigger product recall when a brand name is mentioned – it’s the reverse. When a customer faces a need, the brand should come to mind as the natural solution. Think of Bisleri in India. The brand has become so synonymous with packaged drinking water that consumers often ask for “a Bisleri” regardless of the actual brand in the bottle. That is the power of strong product-perspective identity. However, Aaker also cautions that product attributes tend to be the focus of identity efforts to the exclusion of other perspectives that can add value and distinctiveness– which is why the model pushes strategists further.

### Brand as an organization 🔗

This perspective shifts focus away from the product itself and toward the people, culture, values, and programs that make up the company. Organizational attributes such as innovation, a drive for quality, and concern for the environment are created by the people, culture, values, and programs of the company. Crucially, these attributes are far more durable and harder for competitors to imitate than product features. The Tata Group in India is a textbook example. Tata’s identity as an organization built on trust, national service, and ethical business is nearly impossible to replicate with a product tweak or a marketing campaign. That organizational character becomes a brand asset in its own right.

### Brand as a person 🔗

A brand, like a person, can have a distinct personality. The brand-as-person perspective suggests a brand identity that is richer and more interesting than one based on product attributes alone. Brand personality creates a self-expressive benefit – customers choose brands partly to communicate something about themselves. Aaker’s daughter, Jennifer Aaker, a marketing professor at Stanford, identified five dimensions of brand personality: Sincerity, Excitement, Competence, Sophistication, and Ruggedness. Harley-Davidson leans into Ruggedness and freedom. Apple projects Sophistication and Competence. When a brand’s personality resonates, customers don’t just buy the product – they align with the brand’s character.

### Brand as a symbol 🔗

Symbols give a brand structural cohesion. A strong symbol can provide cohesion and structure to an identity and make it much easier to gain recognition and recall – its absence can be a substantial handicap. Aaker identifies three types of symbols: visual imagery, metaphors, and brand heritage. Nike’s Swoosh is perhaps the most iconic example – a single mark that carries decades of athletic aspiration, without a word of explanation. Brand heritage also lives here: Aaker argues that a brand’s history and longevity can themselves become identity assets, conveying reliability and depth that a new entrant simply cannot manufacture.

Not every brand needs to use all four perspectives. For some brands, only one perspective will be viable and appropriate – but each brand should consider all of them before deciding which are most relevant to its strategy.

## Kapferer’s brand identity prism 🔗

While Aaker’s model is admired for its breadth and flexibility, Jean-Noël Kapferer’s Brand Identity Prism takes a more structured approach. Published in his 1996 book Strategic Brand Management, the prism was designed to address a specific confusion that plagued the industry: the difference between brand identity (what the brand intends to project) and brand image (what consumers actually perceive). Kapferer built a six-faceted model to help brands define and consistently communicate their true identity – not just chase short-term perceptions.

The prism is organized along two axes. The vertical axis separates the Sender (the brand) from the Receiver (the consumer). The horizontal axis separates Externalisation – elements that are visible and outward-facing – from Internalisation – elements that are internal to the brand’s spirit. Both sides must be in place for a brand to create a strong identity, and for a brand to remain strong, it must stay true to that identity.

## The six facets of Kapferer’s prism 🔗

### Physique 🔗

A brand, first and foremost, should have its physique – physical specifications and qualities that immediately come to mind. This includes the logo, color palette, packaging, and flagship product. Physique is the brand’s most external, tangible expression – the part a consumer encounters first. Coca-Cola’s red color and the iconic contour bottle are so deeply embedded in the brand’s physique that altering either would fracture recognition built over more than a century. According to Kapferer, physical appearance is important – but it is not all. Physique sets the stage; the other five facets give it meaning.

### Personality 🔗

Every brand, through its communication style, tone of voice, and choice of spokesperson, develops a character. The way a brand speaks of its products or services shows what kind of person it would be if it were human. Mountain Dew, for instance, consistently aligns itself with thrill-seekers and adventure athletes – its communication has an unmistakably energetic, bold personality. Personality sits on the Sender and Internalisation side of the prism, meaning it reflects what the brand intentionally projects about its own character.

### Culture 🔗

Culture refers to the set of values and principles that underpin everything a brand does. According to Kapferer, culture is the set of values that feed into or set a foundation for the brand – in some cases this includes the culture and values of the brand’s country of origin. Ferrari, for example, is inseparable from the Italian tradition of artisanal performance engineering. Apple, on the other hand, built its culture around a globally resonant idea – the democratization of technology through beautiful design – making culture independent of geography. Culture is an internal driver; it guides how products are made, how employees behave, and what the brand ultimately stands for.

### Relationship 🔗

Brands are not just products – they are a mode of exchange between people and companies. The Relationship facet defines how a brand behaves toward its customers: the nature of the bond it seeks to establish. BMW has a serious-but-playful relationship with its customers, whereas Ferrari’s relationship is more serious and exclusive. In the service sector, this facet is especially powerful. A brand like Southwest Airlines has built its identity on a casual, friendly, almost irreverent relationship with passengers – one that directly differentiates it from more formal competitors.

### Reflection 🔗

Reflection is about the stereotypical customer a brand projects in its marketing – not necessarily who actually buys the product, but who the brand shows using it. Brand reflection is about how marketers choose to portray their target audience – you don’t necessarily need to show those people in your marketing materials, you just need to show people who appeal to your target audience. Nike’s advertisements largely feature elite or aspirational athletes, even though the brand’s actual customer base is far broader. This projected image shapes how the brand is perceived and who feels drawn to it.

### Self-image 🔗

While reflection is external – how the brand portrays the consumer – self-image is internal: how consumers see themselves when they use the brand. If brand reflection is how customers want to be seen outwardly, self-image is how they currently see themselves, inwardly. Parents who buy Volvo see themselves as safety-conscious and responsible. Professionals who carry a Mont Blanc pen see themselves as having arrived. Luxury brands like Porsche and Lamborghini thrive precisely because their customers’ self-images align perfectly with what the brand represents. Tapping into this facet correctly builds loyalty that is nearly immune to price competition.

## Aaker vs. Kapferer: two lenses, one goal 🔗

Both models ultimately pursue the same objective – a brand identity that is clear, differentiated, and enduring. The difference lies in approach. Aaker’s model provides a broader, more adaptable approach that is particularly useful for managing brand portfolios and giving strategists flexibility in which elements to include. Kapferer’s prism, on the other hand, offers a tightly coupled six-facet structure that forces simultaneous attention to both the brand’s intended self and the consumer’s perception. Many practitioners use Aaker for breadth and Kapferer for concise executional guidance– treating them as complementary rather than competing tools.

Used together, these two frameworks offer a remarkably complete picture of what a brand is, what it stands for, and how it lives in the minds of the people it serves.

What do you think? Does a brand you admire align better with Aaker’s multi-perspective approach or Kapferer’s prism structure – and what does that reveal about how the brand has been built? If you were building a brand from scratch today, which model would you reach for first, and why?

Strengthen Identity with the Aaker Brand Identity Model

## Marketing Frameworks >

Aaker Brand Identity Model

# Aaker Brand Identity Model

Visit Umbrex Branding Practice

## 1. What Is Aaker Brand Identity Model?

The Aaker Brand Identity Model—also called the Aaker Brand Identity System—is a comprehensive framework for defining what a brand stands for and how it should be expressed. It helps leaders articulate a brand’s core and extended identity, the value proposition it delivers, and the role it plays in customers’ lives, drawing on four complementary perspectives: brand as product, organization, person, and symbol.

This is a brand strategy framework within the broader family of brand, architecture, and equity models. It is widely used by consultants and corporate brand teams to move beyond a tagline or campaign and codify the enduring elements that guide positioning, design, communications, and portfolio decisions.

In plain terms: the model turns “who we are as a brand” into a structured system—what’s timeless (core identity), what adds richness (extended identity), what we promise (value proposition), and how we show up (personality, symbols, experiences). It becomes the north star for consistent, long-term brand building.

## 2. Origin and Background

Origin: Developed and popularized by David A. Aaker, a marketing scholar and practitioner, in the mid‑1990s—most notably in his 1996 book Building Strong Brands. Aaker previously advanced the field with his 1991 work Managing Brand Equity.

Why it was created: Many organizations treated “brand” as a logo or short-term campaign idea. Aaker introduced a planning model that defines brand identity holistically and provides a durable foundation for strategy, communications, and architecture.

Diffusion: The model is taught in business schools and embedded in consulting and agency methodologies worldwide. It remains a reference point for brand identity work, often adapted to digital and multi-platform contexts.

## 3. How the Aaker Brand Identity Model Works

Aaker’s model is a system, not a single pyramid. It has three tightly connected parts: (1) the Brand Identity System (core and extended identity seen through four perspectives), (2) the Value Proposition and Brand–Customer Relationships, and (3) Brand Positioning (the subset of identity emphasized to compete in a specific market).

### The Brand Identity System

- Core Identity: The timeless essence of the brand—3–5 ideas that should remain stable across products, markets, and time. Think of this as what you would defend at all costs.
- Extended Identity: The richer set of elements that add texture and completeness—personality traits, capabilities, design codes, origins, stories, and associations that bring the brand to life.

Aaker organizes identity elements via four complementary perspectives:

- Brand as Product: Scope, attributes, quality/value, uses, users, and country/region of origin. This grounds the brand in what it offers and to whom.
- Brand as Organization: Culture, values, people, and capabilities. This captures what’s unique about how the firm operates (e.g., innovation discipline, service ethos, sustainability standard).
- Brand as Person: Personality and voice (e.g., bold, meticulous, empathetic), and the type of relationship the brand forms (coach, partner, guardian). This humanizes the brand and guides tone and behavior.
- Brand as Symbol: Visual imagery, metaphors, heritage, and distinctive assets (logos, colors, sonic cues) that aid recognition and memory.

### Value Proposition and Brand–Customer Relationships

- Value Proposition: The benefits the brand promises and delivers—functional (what it does), emotional (how it makes customers feel), and self‑expressive (what it helps them say about themselves). Aaker emphasizes this trio to connect performance to meaning.
- Brand–Customer Relationship: The role the brand plays in people’s lives (e.g., trusted advisor, catalyst, protector), implying expectations for behavior and experience.

### Brand Position

Brand Position is the subset of identity and value proposition actively communicated to a target to achieve advantage in a specific competitive context. Identity is broader and enduring; position is selective and executional.

Put together, the model answers: who we are (identity), what we promise (value), how we behave and signal (personality and symbols), and what we emphasize to win now (position).

## 4. When to Use the Aaker Brand Identity Model

Best suited for:

- Organizations codifying or refreshing brand strategy beyond a campaign, including rebrands, mergers, and global expansions.
- Complex portfolios needing a coherent backbone for sub-brands, endorsements, and design systems.
- B2B and B2C companies that want brand direction to inform product, experience, and culture—not just communications.

Especially powerful when:

- There’s fragmentation across markets or channels and you need a unifying identity with room for local expression.
- Internal culture and capabilities are true differentiators (brand as organization), not just product features.
- You must align leadership and agencies around durable brand building blocks before investing in creative and media.

Less suitable or potentially misleading when:

- You only need a short-term positioning for a single product variant; lighter tools (e.g., positioning statement) may suffice.
- Brand architecture is undecided. Identity work benefits from clarity on portfolio roles; address architecture in parallel.
- Teams treat identity as slogans rather than as guidance for behavior, experience, and proof—leading to surface-level outputs.

Practice note: The model remains widely used. Contemporary teams integrate it with customer data (JTBD, analytics), precision around distinctive assets, and governance mechanisms to ensure identity shows up consistently across digital journeys and partner ecosystems.

## 5. How to Apply the Aaker Brand Identity Model: Step-by-Step

Clarify scope, role, and stakeholders.

Define the brand level (corporate, master, sub‑brand, solution), geographies, and time horizon (3–5 years). Align on decisions this identity must inform (positioning, naming, architecture, design system). Assemble cross‑functional leadership (brand/marketing, product, HR, sales, regions).

Conduct strategic brand analysis.

Use three lenses: customer (segments, needs/jobs, perceptions, drivers), competitor (positions, codes, equities), and self (capabilities, culture, purpose, proof). Inputs: qual/quant research, win/loss, brand tracking, employee insight, financials, and audit of distinctive assets.

Draft the core identity (3–5 elements).

Synthesize non‑negotiables that define the brand across time and offers. Test for durability (“will this still be true in five years?”), distinctiveness (“ownable vs category generic”), and breadth (“guides the whole brand, not a product feature”).

Build the extended identity using the four perspectives.

For each perspective—product, organization, person, symbol—list 4–6 elements, then prioritize 2–3 that best amplify the core. Ensure each is evidenced (e.g., culture behaviors, certifications, design codes, origin story) and actionable (guides choices).

Define the value proposition.

Codify the functional, emotional, and self‑expressive benefits the brand promises to its priority audiences. Link each benefit to proof (features, outcomes, assets) and ensure benefits ladder logically from attributes to meaning.

Articulate the brand–customer relationship.

Decide the role you play (coach/provocateur/guardian/ally) based on customer needs and your culture. Translate this into tone, service principles, and experience standards.

Choose the competitive brand position.

Select the subset of identity and benefits to emphasize for your primary segment and market. Validate with perceptual maps, message testing, and pricing research. Ensure the position is credible, relevant, and differentiated.

Align brand architecture (if in scope).

Define how the identity cascades across portfolio elements (branded house, sub‑brands, endorsements). Specify what is shared (core, codes) and what flexes (personality notes, proof, language) by offer or region.

Codify distinctive assets and executional cues.

Translate identity into design (logo rules, color, typography, imagery, motion, sonic), voice and narrative, and service/experience standards. Identify assets to protect and strengthen through consistent use.

Governance and capability enablement.

Publish guidelines and playbooks, designate owners, set up review councils, and establish tooling (DAM, templates, component libraries). Train teams and agencies; define escalation for exceptions.

Measure and refresh.

Set KPIs (awareness, consideration, associations, NPS, price realization, CLV). Track distinctiveness and linkage of assets. Refresh extended identity elements as markets evolve while protecting the core.

## 6. Example: Aaker Brand Identity Model in Action

Company: “HeliosHealth,” a $3.5B global health technology firm expanding from hospital equipment into connected home health devices and software.

Problem: The corporate brand was respected in clinical equipment but perceived as cold and institutional by consumers. The portfolio was proliferating (apps, wearables, services) with inconsistent naming and visuals. Leadership needed a unifying identity that could stretch from B2B to B2C, guide architecture, and support a clear competitive position.

Applying the model:

Extended identity:

- As Product: Integrated ecosystem, data‑driven insights, interoperability.
- As Organization: Safety culture, privacy by design, clinician–designer co‑creation.
- As Person: Calm, clear, encouraging (tone guidelines and examples).
- As Symbol: New “calm light” visual motif, soft palette, distinct chime for device/app interactions.

Outcomes: Within nine months, brand tracking showed a 14‑point lift in “easy to use” among consumers and a 10‑point lift in “clinically trustworthy” among clinicians. Consistent assets improved digital recall; conversion on DTC landing pages increased 18%. The identity system streamlined creative production and clarified portfolio roles, reducing duplicate builds and agency rework.

## 7. Strengths and Limitations

### Strengths

- Architecture: Branded house with descriptive solution names; one endorsed sub‑brand for a regulated clinician platform. Shared design system across touchpoints.
- Holistic and durable: Balances timeless core with rich extended elements—useful across products, markets, and time.
- Actionable breadth: The four perspectives integrate product reality, organizational culture, personality, and symbols—bridging strategy and execution.
- Connects to value: Explicit focus on functional, emotional, and self‑expressive benefits links brand to outcomes customers care about.
- Clarifies position vs. identity: Avoids conflating long‑term identity with short‑term positioning choices.
- Portfolio‑friendly: Provides a backbone for architecture and extension decisions.

### Limitations

- Complexity risk: Without prioritization, extended identity can become a laundry list that confuses teams.
- Subjectivity: If not grounded in research and proof, identity statements can drift into aspiration rather than reality.
- Governance demands: The system requires discipline to embed in design, content, product, and culture.
- Not a substitute for strategy: It frames who you are; it does not set market focus, pricing, or channel choices on its own.

## 8. Common Pitfalls (and How to Avoid Them)

Confusing identity with messaging or campaigns.

What goes wrong: Teams craft taglines instead of defining enduring identity, causing rework each campaign cycle.

How to avoid: Separate long‑term identity (core/extended) from short‑term messaging; let identity guide but not equal copy.

Generic core identity.

What goes wrong: Words like “innovative” and “customer‑centric” signal nothing distinct.

How to avoid: Pressure‑test for specificity and proof; ban generic terms unless uniquely evidenced.

Skipping the “brand as organization” lens.

What goes wrong: Identity ignores culture and capabilities—promises can’t be delivered.

How to avoid: Include behaviors, systems, and talent as part of identity; tie to operating principles.

Overstuffed extended identity.

What goes wrong: Too many elements create contradictions and inconsistency.

How to avoid: Prioritize a small set per perspective; codify “do more of/never do” rules.

Weak linkage between benefits and proof.

What goes wrong: Emotional claims without functional evidence erode credibility.

How to avoid: Pair each benefit with reasons‑to‑believe (data, certifications, case studies, demos).

Identity that doesn’t travel.

What goes wrong: Global/local tensions cause fragmentation.

How to avoid: Define what is core and non‑negotiable vs. what flexes by market; provide toolkits and examples.

No governance or metrics.

What goes wrong: Identity drifts over time; assets are under‑leveraged.

How to avoid: Establish owners, processes, and KPIs; audit asset distinctiveness and linkage regularly.

## 9. How the Aaker Brand Identity Model Relates to Other Frameworks

- Keller’s Customer‑Based Brand Equity (CBBE) Pyramid: CBBE focuses on building blocks from salience to resonance (how equity forms in minds). Aaker focuses on defining identity and value (what the brand stands for). Use Aaker to define; use CBBE to track how equity accumulates.
- Kapferer’s Brand Identity Prism: Another identity model with six facets (physique, personality, culture, relationship, reflection, self‑image). Substantial overlap; some teams prefer Prism’s symmetry. Aaker’s four perspectives and core/extended split can be more execution‑friendly for portfolios.
- Positioning Statement Framework: Compresses identity into a one‑sentence competitive stance for a target. Identity is broader; positioning is a selective emphasis.
- Benefit Ladder: Operationalizes the value proposition (functional, emotional, self‑expressive) within Aaker’s system—use it to connect attributes to higher‑order meaning.
- Brand Architecture (Branded House vs House of Brands): Identity informs what should be shared versus distinct across the portfolio; architecture decisions, in turn, affect how identity scales.
- Perceptual Mapping: Reveals current perceptions and white spaces. Use it to stress‑test whether your chosen position reflects and can shift market perceptions.

Choice guidance: Start with customer and competitive insight; define identity with Aaker; articulate position for priority segments; design architecture for scale; track equity with CBBE; and use perceptual maps and benefit ladders for activation and validation.

## 10. Key Takeaways

- The Aaker Brand Identity Model defines enduring brand identity (core and extended) through four perspectives—product, organization, person, symbol—and links it to a clear value proposition and brand–customer relationship.
- Identity is broader and more durable than positioning; position is the subset of identity emphasized to win in a given market.
- Strength comes from specificity and proof—avoid generic words; ground benefits in evidence and capabilities.
- Use the model to guide architecture, design systems, tone, and experience—not just messaging.
- Prioritize, govern, and measure; refresh extended elements as markets evolve while protecting the core.

## 11. FAQs About the Aaker Brand Identity Model

Is the Aaker model still relevant in digital, fast‑moving markets? Yes. If anything, digital fragmentation makes an enduring identity more valuable. Modern application emphasizes distinctive assets, tone systems for multi‑channel content, and governance to keep identity consistent across partners and platforms.

How is Aaker different from Keller’s CBBE Pyramid? Aaker helps you define what the brand stands for (identity, value proposition, personality, symbols). Keller explains how brand equity is built in customers’ minds (salience → performance/imagery → judgments/feelings → resonance). They are complementary—define with Aaker, track and plan building with Keller.

Can B2B brands use the Aaker model effectively? Absolutely. The “brand as organization” lens is especially powerful for B2B (culture, capabilities, reliability). Value propositions should tie to outcomes (risk, efficiency, growth) and the relationship role (trusted advisor, enabler) across long buying cycles.

How many elements should go into the core identity? Aim for 3–5. Fewer risks being too narrow; more dilutes focus. Each should be specific, evidence‑backed, and resilient across products and markets.

Where does brand purpose fit? Purpose can sit within the core identity (why you exist) and the “brand as organization” perspective. It should inform behavior and decisions, not just communications. Ground it in credible commitments and proof.

How long does a robust identity program take? Typically 8–12 weeks for mid‑sized organizations: 2–3 for analysis, 3–4 for identity development and validation, 2–3 for codification and governance setup. Complex portfolios or global rollouts may take longer, especially if architecture is in scope.

Define Brand Identity with Kapferer Brand Identity Prism

## Marketing Frameworks >

Kapferer Brand Identity Prism

# Kapferer Brand Identity Prism

Visit Umbrex Branding Practice

## What Is the Kapferer Brand Identity Prism?

The Kapferer Brand Identity Prism is a brand strategy framework that defines a brand’s identity through six interlocking facets: Physique, Personality, Culture, Relationship, Reflection, and Self‑image. It helps leaders articulate what a brand is—its essence and expression—rather than what customers merely perceive or how they behave. In short, it is a structured way to codify the brand’s “source code” so that all touchpoints consistently convey who the brand is and what it stands for.

Within the Marketing function—specifically in brand, architecture & equity work—the Prism is a foundational identity tool. Consultants and brand leaders use it to clarify positioning, align internal and external expressions, guide creative development, and manage brand portfolios. Where demand-funnel models focus on customer response, the Prism centers on the brand’s intended identity and the coherent signals it must send.

Executives value the Prism because it translates abstract ideas like “brand essence” into a practical, shared language. It ensures product, design, communications, sales, and culture all tell the same story—over time and across markets.

## Origin and Background

The Brand Identity Prism was developed by Professor Jean‑Noël Kapferer and introduced in his work on strategic brand management in the 1990s. It was popularized globally through his books “Strategic Brand Management” and later “The New Strategic Brand Management,” which have become staples in business schools and executive programs.

Why it was created: Marketers often confused brand identity (what the brand intends to stand for) with brand image (how it is currently perceived). The Prism was designed to separate and structure identity so organizations could build long-term brand coherence rather than chase short-term perceptions. It spread through academic curricula, agency methodologies, and consulting practices, and remains a go-to tool in positioning and brand architecture engagements.

## How the Kapferer Brand Identity Prism Works

The Prism articulates brand identity via six facets that, together, form a coherent whole. Think of it as a 360-degree charter: three facets are more externally expressed (how the brand presents and relates), and three are more internal (the brand’s character and guiding beliefs). Another useful lens contrasts the “picture of the sender” (the brand itself) with the “picture of the recipient” (the typical user and how they see themselves).

### The Six Facets

- Physique (tangible signatures)
- - What are the brand’s defining physical characteristics and “codes”? Logos, colors, shapes, sounds, packaging forms, product signatures, interface patterns—assets that make the brand recognizable at a glance.
- Purpose: Anchor recognition and distinctiveness. Physique is the most visible manifestation of identity and a major driver of mental availability when used consistently.
- Personality (tone and character)
- - If the brand were a person, how would it speak and behave? Confident, witty, meticulous, rebellious, caring?
- Purpose: Guide voice, copy, design style, and behavior so the brand feels consistent across channels and situations.
- Culture (beliefs and values)
- - The brand’s internal compass: beliefs, origins, craft, standards, and purpose. Culture informs what the brand will and will not do.
- Purpose: Align organization and partners; ensure actions match claims. Culture makes “purpose” operational, not performative.
- Relationship (role with customers)
- - The kind of relationship the brand seeks: coach, concierge, companion, challenger, guardian, platform host, etc.
- Purpose: Direct experience design, service models, and policies (e.g., guarantees, support tone, community rules) to embody the intended relationship.
- Reflection (picture of the typical user)
- - Who is depicted as the brand’s prototypical user or usage situation? Demographics, lifestyle, professional context.
- Purpose: Guide storytelling and targeting without stereotyping the actual customer base; reflection is an outward mirror, not a limiting persona list.
- Self‑image (how customers see themselves)
- - How users aspire to view themselves when they use the brand: capable, creative, eco‑conscious, sophisticated, youthful, in control, generous.
- Purpose: Shape emotional resonance and motivate choice by aligning with identity needs and aspirations.

### Structural Principles

- Externalization vs. internalization: Physique, Relationship, and Reflection are largely outward-facing expressions; Personality, Culture, and Self‑image are inward-facing drivers that inform consistent expression.
- Sender vs. recipient: Physique, Personality, and Culture describe the “brand as sender.” Reflection and Self‑image relate to the “customer as recipient.” Relationship bridges the two.
- Coherence over time: The Prism is designed for durability. While campaigns come and go, the six facets—when well defined—provide long-term continuity and room for evolution.

In practice, teams document each facet with concise statements and evidence (assets, rituals, behaviors). The output becomes a central reference for creative briefs, product decisions, service standards, hiring, and partner selection—ensuring every expression of the brand is intentional and mutually reinforcing.

## When to Use the Kapferer Brand Identity Prism

Most helpful for:

- Positioning and re-positioning: Articulating or refreshing what the brand stands for, beyond taglines or campaign themes.
- Brand architecture and portfolio management: Differentiating master brands, sub‑brands, and endorsements; preventing internal cannibalization or identity blur.
- Merger, acquisition, or partnership branding: Reconciling identities and choosing which facets to preserve, evolve, or retire.
- Experience and service design: Translating identity into behavior, tone, and policies across the journey.
- Global/local alignment: Providing a global core while allowing local expressions that still fit the Prism.
- Employer brand and culture programs: Ensuring internal values and behaviors mirror the external promise.

Company contexts: Applicable across B2C and B2B; product and service businesses; start-ups to multinationals. Especially valuable when multiple teams or geographies must act in concert.

Data and time: A focused identity refresh can be done in 3–5 weeks; deeper work with research, co‑creation, and portfolio implications typically spans 8–12+ weeks.

Especially powerful when: An organization needs a durable north star that connects purpose, product, go‑to‑market, and creative into one coherent system—anchoring long-term brand building while accommodating agile execution.

Less effective or risky when: Teams treat the Prism as wordsmithing rather than making real choices; when it is created without customer and employee insight; or when it is divorced from experience and operations, resulting in “say–do” gaps.

## How to Apply the Kapferer Prism: Step‑by‑Step

Clarify the decision and scope

What problem will the identity solve (e.g., fragmentation across sub‑brands, low distinctiveness, inconsistent tone)? Define markets, segments, and time horizon. Identify the touchpoints in scope (product, service, digital, retail, comms) and the degree of change you can realistically implement.

Assemble a cross‑functional team and align on outcomes

Include marketing, product, service, HR, and key regions. Agree on what success looks like: clearer briefs, stronger distinctiveness, improved consideration, higher NPS/retention, culture alignment.

Gather inputs: insight and evidence

Combine external and internal sources:

Draft the current‑state Prism

Populate each facet with concise, evidence‑backed statements and examples (e.g., “Physique: cobalt blue + circular device silhouette; sonic logo at 3 notes; curved UI tiles”). Identify inconsistencies, gaps, and contradictions across facets and markets.

Identify tensions and root causes

Look for misalignments (e.g., “caring” Personality but punitive policies; eco‑Culture claims but non‑recyclable packaging; youthful Reflection but luxury pricing). Prioritize issues that most undermine distinctiveness or trust.

Define the target‑state Prism

Make sharp choices. For each facet, craft statements that are specific, differentiating, and actionable. Stress‑test against competitors (does it sound like anyone else?), feasibility (can we deliver it in product/service?), and longevity (will it endure beyond a campaign?).

Translate identity into codes, behaviors, and policies

Convert each facet into executional guardrails and requirements:

Integrate with positioning and architecture

Ensure the Prism reinforces your positioning (frame of reference; points of parity; points of difference) and clarifies roles across the portfolio (master brand vs. sub‑brands vs. endorsements). Decide which facets are shared centrally and which can localize.

Codify and socialize

Publish a concise brand book: the Prism, rationale, codes, examples, and “before/after” illustrations. Run workshops for marketing, product, service, and agency partners. Establish a governance model (review cadence, approvers, training).

Embed measurement and iterate

Track asset recognition, tone consistency, and behavioral adherence; link to outcomes (consideration, price premium, NPS/retention, community health). Review quarterly; refine the Prism as the business evolves, preserving core identity while updating expression.

1. - Customer insight: attitudes, needs, aspirations, usage occasions, typical user images, self‑image aspirations.
- Brand audit: asset recognition (distinctive brand assets), tone consistency, CX behaviors, community norms, employer brand signals.
- Competitive scan: identity codes competitors own; whitespace and table stakes in the category.
- Cultural audit: founding story, values, rituals, decision principles; what employees believe the brand stands for today.
2. - Physique: Distinctive brand assets (colors, shapes, type, motion, sound); packaging/industrial design codes; UI/UX patterns.
- Personality: Voice and tone system; writing/visual style; do’s/don’ts; training for creators and frontline teams.
- Culture: Principles for product decisions, sourcing, hiring, recognition; proof actions that make values visible.
- Relationship: Service standards, guarantees, conversation etiquette, community moderation, escalation principles.
- Reflection: Guidance on casting, contexts, and stories that signal the intended user without stereotyping.
- Self‑image: Emotional outcomes to evoke; design cues and rituals that help users feel the promised “self.”

## Example: The Prism in Action

Context: A $850M premium coffee brand is expanding from whole‑bean retail into ready‑to‑drink (RTD) cold brew and café experiences across North America and Asia. Growth has plateaued, and creative is inconsistent across markets.

Problem: The brand is known for “quality beans” but lacks a unifying identity that travels across channels (packaged goods, cafes, digital). Regional teams use divergent tones—from “hipster craft” to “luxury lifestyle”—confusing consumers and partners.

Applying the Prism:

- Physique: Audit reveals strong recognition of a distinctive copper color and serif wordmark on bags, but RTD packaging diluted these codes with trend graphics. Decision: codify copper + textured paper + embossed seal across pack and café signage; introduce a signature cup silhouette.
- Personality: Set as “obsessive yet welcoming.” Voice principles: precise, sensory language; no snobbery; confident brevity.
- Culture: Rooted in craftsmanship and ethical sourcing. Proof actions: publish farm‑level transparency reports; commit to living‑income benchmarks; invest in training baristas as “craft educators.”
- Relationship: “Mentor host.” In cafés and digital, the brand guides discovery—flight tastings, brewing lessons, seasonal origin stories—without lecturing.
- Reflection: Typical user portrayed as curious urban professionals and creators seeking mindful rituals—shown in diverse contexts (home brewing, studio breaks, café meetups).
- Self‑image: “I am discerning yet open‑minded.” Customers feel quietly confident, not flashy, when choosing the brand.

Actions: Redesign RTD packaging to restore copper + seal codes; introduce a sonic pour sound in ads; standardize café service rituals (origin cards, flight intros); update tone guidelines; launch a “Craft Transparency” microsite with supply data; train staff on the mentor‑host relationship model.

Outcomes (12 months): Distinctive asset recall for copper + seal rises 18 points; consideration in RTD grows 9 points; café NPS improves by 11 points; price premium holds despite category promotions; brand tracking shows clearer typical‑user reflection and stronger self‑image alignment in both regions.

## Strengths and Limitations

### Strengths

- Holistic and enduring: Integrates tangible, emotional, cultural, and relational elements into a single, durable identity system.
- Actionable coherence: Converts identity into clear codes, tones, behaviors, and policies—useful for creative briefs and experience design.
- Alignment across functions and geographies: Creates a common language that travels from HQ to local teams and from marketing to operations and HR.
- Portfolio clarity: Helps differentiate roles across master and sub‑brands, reducing overlap and internal cannibalization.

### Limitations

- Not a market choice tool: The Prism does not decide where to play or set competitive strategy; it expresses identity within those choices.
- Risk of abstraction: Poorly facilitated sessions can produce vague adjectives detached from product or service reality.
- Measurement gap: Identity coherence is harder to measure than awareness or conversion; requires disciplined proxies and behavioral indicators.
- Static temptation: Treating the Prism as fixed can miss shifts in culture, category norms, or business model—identity should be stable but not rigid.

## Common Pitfalls (and How to Avoid Them)

Word salad over specificity

What goes wrong: Generic adjectives (“innovative,” “premium”) that any competitor could claim.

Avoid it: Demand proof and manifestation: “What will a customer see, hear, or feel that only we do?” Tie each facet to assets, behaviors, and policies.

Ignoring Culture

What goes wrong: Aspirational identity conflicts with internal reality; promises outpace delivery.

Avoid it: Define non‑negotiable values and the operational choices that express them (sourcing, SLAs, hiring). Show receipts.

Confusing Reflection with target segment

What goes wrong: Narrow casting that alienates broader buyers; stereotyping in creative.

Avoid it: Treat Reflection as a symbolic portrait for storytelling, not a literal demographic box.

Misaligning Relationship and policies

What goes wrong: “Helpful” tone paired with rigid returns or punitive fees undermines trust.

Avoid it: Audit policies and service design against the intended relationship; fix contradictions first.

Letting agencies “interpret” without guardrails

What goes wrong: Divergent executions across markets and channels.

Avoid it: Provide a codified Prism, examples, and review gates. Train partners on personality and relationship behaviors, not just visual assets.

One‑and‑done identity decks

What goes wrong: Identity freezes while category and culture evolve.

Avoid it: Annual reviews to test relevance; evolve expression while protecting core facets.

## How the Prism Relates to Other Frameworks

- STP (Segmentation–Targeting–Positioning): STP sets “who and what promise.” The Prism expresses “who we are” to deliver that promise—codifying assets, tone, and behaviors that make the positioning live.
- Keller’s CBBE/Brand Resonance: CBBE explains how equity builds from salience to resonance through customer perceptions and behaviors. The Prism defines the brand’s identity inputs that, consistently expressed, should create those downstream perceptions and behaviors.
- Aaker’s Brand Identity System: Aaker organizes brand identity into core/extended identity and brand-as-product/organization/person/symbol. Kapferer’s Prism offers a tightly coupled six‑facet structure. Many use Aaker for breadth and Kapferer for concise executional guidance.
- Perceptual mapping and positioning canvases: Maps show where brands sit relative to attributes; the Prism ensures your chosen position is expressed coherently in assets and experiences.
- Distinctive Brand Assets and Category Entry Points: Byron Sharp’s work focuses on mental/physical availability. The Prism helps choose and codify assets (Physique) and craft occasions and user imagery (Reflection) that cue entry points.
- Brand architecture frameworks: Architecture decides where equity resides across a portfolio. The Prism clarifies which identity facets are shared at master brand level vs. differentiated in sub‑brands.

## Key Takeaways

- The Kapferer Brand Identity Prism is a six‑facet framework that codifies a brand’s identity so every touchpoint tells the same story.
- It balances external expression (Physique, Relationship, Reflection) with internal drivers (Personality, Culture, Self‑image) to ensure coherence.
- Use it to align positioning, creative, experience, and portfolio roles—especially when multiple regions or teams must execute consistently.
- Its power lies in turning abstract identity into tangible assets, behaviors, and policies; its risk is becoming vague if not tied to proof.
- Complement it with STP for market choices and with CBBE/Resonance to track customer perceptions and loyalty over time.

## FAQs About the Kapferer Brand Identity Prism

### Is the Prism still relevant in digital and omnichannel contexts?

Yes. If anything, it’s more relevant. Digital multiplies touchpoints and teams; the Prism ensures voice, design, and behavior stay coherent across product, service, social, retail, and community. Update expressions for channels, but protect the core facets.

### How is the Prism different from Keller’s CBBE Pyramid?

The Prism defines the brand’s intended identity (inputs). CBBE describes how customer perceptions and behaviors (outputs) build equity from awareness to resonance. Use the Prism to decide what to express; use CBBE to diagnose whether the market is receiving it and where equity is stalling.

### Can B2B and employer brands use the Prism?

Absolutely. In B2B, Relationship and Culture are often decisive (trust, reliability, ethics). For employer brands, Personality and Culture guide hiring and rituals, while Reflection/Self‑image align with employee identity and pride.

### How long does it take to build or refresh a Prism?

A focused refresh can be done in 3–5 weeks. Complex, multi‑market identities with research, portfolio implications, and governance setup typically require 8–12+ weeks.

### How do we measure whether the Prism is working?

Track identity coherence and business impact: distinctive asset recognition, tone and behavior adherence, experience audits, plus outcomes such as consideration, price premium, NPS/retention, and community health. Use pre/post tests and holdouts where feasible.

# Customer-based brand equity (CBBE) models: Keller vs. Aaker

Oct 23, 2020

We use customer-based brand equity (CBBE) to show how a brand’s success can be directly attributed to customers’ attitudes towards it. What is it, and how can it help you build your brand?

Share

## What is customer-based brand equity (CBBE)?

Apple. Coca-Cola. Tylenol. Porsche. What do you feel when you see the names of these brands? They all provoke feelings (positive, their marketing teams hope) and are examples of strong brands that enjoy outstanding brand equity.

CBBE is the value of a brand, based on what customers feel about and think of it. Brand equity was traditionally built through word of mouth recommendation. Now, social media, online advertising and customer experience have enhanced the potential for reaching customers on a more personal, emotional level and creating a relationship with them. It’s essential that your customers’ perceptions, feelings, thoughts, and experiences regarding your brand are always positive.

## Keller’s brand equity model

Because brand equity as a single concept is subtle, nuanced and difficult to quantify, it’s best approached in measurable stages, using a model. The best-known CBBE model is the Keller Model, devised by Professor of Marketing Kevin Lane Keller and originally published in his mighty Strategic Brand Management.

The Keller model is a pyramid shape and shows businesses how to build from a strong foundation of brand identity upwards towards the holy grail of brand equity ‘resonance’. This is where customers are in a sufficiently positive relationship with a brand to be advocates for it.

## What exactly is the customer-based brand equity pyramid?

Each stage of the pyramid builds upon the one before, so it’s important to cement each step before moving on to the higher stages. Every experience along a customer’s journey with your brand should leave them with positive thoughts, emotions, and beliefs.

Working up to the resonance level affords a brand opportunities to recognize and capitalize on its customers’ loyalties and attitudes – whether they are positive or negative. Hearing about negative experiences help a brand understand how their customers feel about their product, so they can flip them into positive experiences.

By dividing CBBE into Keller’s four levels, marketers can understand what their customers want and need before they’ve even bought the product, or maybe even before they know they want it.

The iPad is a stunning example of this CBBE: from the robust foundation of Apple’s brand identity, the iPad was developed to look great, be easy to use, do everything its customers wanted, and more. Customers loved it and any glitches that attracted negative responses were quickly patched.

Before long, iPad users were extolling its virtues and their customer loyalty, and the iPad is now ubiquitous in stores, health centers, schools, offices and homes. It’s a classic example of something we didn’t know we needed or wanted until we saw one. Now we can’t do without it.

## How the four levels of Keller’s CBBE pyramid work:

### Level 1: Brand Identity (who are you?)

We can add to this question: ‘and what makes you unique?’ This is how customers look at your brand and distinguish it from others. It’s the most important level and must be strong to support the rest of the pyramid above it. Its role is twofold:

- To identify your USP (unique selling point) in the marketplace
- To let customers know who you are

It explores the words and images buyers associate with when they hear a particular brand name. Brand identity quantifies the breadth and depth of customer awareness of a brand.

#### What brand managers can do in Level 1:

- Identify your USP – why would you choose your brand over the competition?
- Conduct market research to identify the wants and needs of your target audience
- Target your customers with channeled ad campaigns (social media, Google) to ensure they know who you are and understand your USP

### Level 2: Brand Meaning (what are you?)

Once customers become aware of your brand, they’ll want to know more about your product. They’ll question its features, looks and style, reliability, durability, customer experience and value for money, to find its brand meaning. It’s important to deliver quality and reliability every time, to create positive brand associations in the customers’ minds. For the purposes of brand reputation, Level 2 is split into two categories:

1. Brand performance (rational): This either builds a brand, or breaks it. It covers product functionality, reliability, durability, and price as well as customer service and satisfaction. It’s ‘it does what it says on the tin’ territory and when it performs well, customer opinion will be positive.
2. Brand imagery (emotional): different, but equally important, imagery meets the customers’ social and psychological needs. What does the brand appear to be to customers? Volvo appears Scandi-chic, family-orientated, safe and eco-responsible; Cushelle soft, homely and cozy.

#### What brand managers can do in Level 2:

- Check that your product or service is living up to its advertised promises by analyzing negative reviews, negative comments, refunds and returns
- Fix the negatives!
- Exceed expectations by giving customers value add-ons such as freebies or anniversary discounts
- Make sure your advertising and imagery truly reflects the product experience– it doesn’t over-promise and under-deliver.
- Be prepared to develop packaging, logo, consistent visual advertising and customer service.

### Level 3: Brand Response (What are the feelings for the brand?)

On this level of Keller’s model, judgment and feelings can be hard to separate and are intensely personal for each individual customer.

- One customer may judge the brand irrelevant to them, whereas another will find it completely relevant.
- Another may make their own value comparison against another product, harshly or fairly.

And add to the mix actual interaction and perceived reputation and you can see how hard it can be to quantify how customers feel about a brand and how much they trust it.

#### What brand managers can do in Level 3:

- Track your customer feedback across social media channels and other data sources to identify pain points and areas of customer dissatisfaction
- Fix things that flag up as negative
- Run brand perception surveys
- Give special offers and discounts to strengthen customers’ emotional bond with your brand

### Level 4: Brand Resonance (a strong relationship)

The apex of Keller’s CBBE model is resonance, when a customer is:

- Loyal to a brand
- Considers it superior
- Will buy no other
- May join a brand community, such as a social media group or club
- Advocates its merits to others

Many things resonate with customers: lifetime experience, customer service, products and value. A good measure for resonance is the Net Promoter Score that asks one simple question: “How likely is it that you would recommend [Product X] to a friend or colleague?”.

#### What brand managers can do in Level 4:

- Everything you can to keep loyal customers at the top of the pyramid!
- Treat Level 4 customers as a community of VIPs – offer quality extras, such as exclusive rewards, free gifts, member-only events and discounts, preferential upgrades or shipping
- Find out why customers reached the resonance level
- Don’t rest on your laurels – keep improving that customer experience that led to customers reaching resonance

Keller’s model is deceptively beautiful in its simplicity; building customer-based brand equity is, in reality, a long and hard road. When you start at the bottom with a great brand identity, then get customers to know your brand and your business gradually, you’ll create a brand that people will like, trust and which will ultimately be successful.

## Aaker’s brand equity model: A second theory

Whereas the Keller brand equity model focuses largely on emotions, Professor David Aaker says it’s much simpler than that: it’s all about recognition. The most successful brands are those that drive recognition (think Mickey Mouse for Disney) in the emotional part of the brain that makes split-second decisions about what to buy.

Aaker sees brand equity as a mixture of brand awareness, brand associations and brand loyalty. All these add up to the value provided by a brand’s goods or services. The Aaker Model helps to create a brand strategy made up of various components that separate a brand from its competition and advance it.

Aaker says that there are five components of controlling brand equity. The higher the data scores for these, the closer the product is to achieving brand equity:

- Brand awareness: how known is the brand to the public? Like the Keller model, this is the starting point of building brand equity.
- Brand loyalty: how loyal are people to the brand? Loyalty is hard for competitors to copy, so it gives a brand time to respond to competition.
- Perceived quality: is the brand known or expected to deliver good quality products? Quality above features will give a product the edge with consumers – for a while, until they begin to demand the features.
- Brand associations: what do people feel when they see the brand? The cognitive, split-second reaction to seeing the brand on adverts, during the buying process, the ‘feel-good factor’, the number of available brand extensions and differentiations.
- Patents, IP and trading partners: brands with higher accumulated proprietary rights have a competitive edge against other brands.

All these components are measurable when ran through the right platforms that highlight where more could be done to attain brand equity. Branding needs to be delivered at every touchpoint along the customer journey to ensure this recognition. Data can then be gathered at various stages of marketing to inform and increase customer brand loyalty and show up the distinctiveness of the brand from its competitors.

1. Brand performance (rational): This either builds a brand, or breaks it. It covers product functionality, reliability, durability, and price as well as customer service and satisfaction. It’s ‘it does what it says on the tin’ territory and when it performs well, customer opinion will be positive.
2. Brand imagery (emotional): different, but equally important, imagery meets the customers’ social and psychological needs. What does the brand appear to be to customers? Volvo appears Scandi-chic, family-orientated, safe and eco-responsible; Cushelle soft, homely and cosy.

#### What brand managers can do in Level 2:

- Check that your product or service is living up to its advertised promises by analysing negative reviews, negative comments, refunds and returns
- Fix the negatives!
- Exceed expectations by giving customers value add-ons such as freebies or anniversary discounts
- Make sure your advertising and imagery truly reflects the product experience– it doesn’t over-promise and under-deliver.
- Be prepared to develop packaging, logo, consistent visual advertising and customer service.

### Level 3: Brand Response (What are the feelings for the brand?)

On this level of Keller’s model, judgement and feelings can be hard to separate and are intensely personal for each individual customer.

- One customer may judge the brand irrelevant to them, whereas another will find it completely relevant.
- Another may make their own value comparison against another product, harshly or fairly.

And add to the mix actual interaction and perceived reputation and you can see how hard it can be to quantify how customers feel about a brand and how much they trust it.

#### What brand managers can do in Level 3:

- Track your customer feedback across social media channels and other data sources to identify pain points and areas of customer dissatisfaction.
- Fix things that flag up as negative
- Run brand perception surveys
- Give special offers and discounts to strengthen customers’ emotional bond with your brand

### Level 4: Brand Resonance (a strong relationship)

The apex of Keller’s CBBE model is resonance, when a customer is:

- Loyal to a brand
- Considers it superior
- Will buy no other
- May join a brand community, such as a social media group or club
- Advocates its merits to others

Many things resonate with customers: lifetime experience, customer service, products and value. A good measure for resonance is the Net Promoter Score that asks one simple question: “How likely is it that you would recommend [Product X] to a friend or colleague?”.

#### What brand managers can do in Level 4:

- Everything you can to keep loyal customers at the top of the pyramid!
- Treat Level 4 customers as a community of VIPs – offer quality extras, such as exclusive rewards, free gifts, member-only events and discounts, preferential upgrades or shipping
- Find out why customers reached the resonance level
- Don’t rest on your laurels – keep improving that customer experience that led to customers reaching resonance

Keller’s model is deceptively beautiful in its simplicity; building customer-based brand equity is, in reality, a long and hard road. When you start at the bottom with a great brand identity, then get customers to know your brand and your business gradually, you’ll create a brand that people will like, trust and which will ultimately be successful.

## Aaker’s brand equity model: A second theory

Whereas the Keller brand equity model focuses largely on emotions, Professor David Aaker says it’s much simpler than that: it’s all about recognition. The most successful brands are those that drive recognition (think Mickey Mouse for Disney) in the emotional part of the brain that makes split-second decisions about what to buy.

Aaker sees brand equity as a mixture of brand awareness, brand associations and brand loyalty. All these add up to the value provided by a brand’s goods or services. The Aaker Model helps to create a brand strategy made up of various components that separate a brand from its competition and advance it.

Aaker says that there are five components of controlling brand equity. The higher the data scores for these, the closer the product is to achieving brand equity:

- Brand awareness: how known is the brand to the public? Like the Keller model, this is the starting point of building brand equity.
- Brand loyalty: how loyal are people to the brand? Loyalty is hard for competitors to copy, so it gives a brand time to respond to competition.
- Perceived quality: is the brand known or expected to deliver good quality products? Quality above features will give a product the edge with consumers – for a while, until they begin to demand the features.
- Brand associations: what do people feel when they see the brand? The cognitive, split-second reaction to seeing the brand on adverts, during the buying process, the ‘feel-good factor’, the number of available brand extensions and differentiations.
- Patents, IP and trading partners: brands with higher accumulated proprietary rights have a competitive edge against other brands.

All these components are measurable when run through the right platforms that highlight where more could be done to attain brand equity. Branding needs to be delivered at every touchpoint along the customer journey to ensure this recognition. Data can then be gathered at various stages of marketing to inform and increase customer brand loyalty and show up the distinctiveness of the brand from its competitors.

## What Is the Aaker Brand Equity Model? Definition and Components

By Angela Kayode-Sanni | Last updated:

### Introduction

The general perception of a brand or a brand personality is essential in the business world. A study has shown that customers expect more from the brands they use in terms of customer experience, their work culture, the environment where their products are made, and so on.

In other to keep up with customer expectations, organizations now need to see how their marketing efforts can contribute to their brand equity and boost their brand image.

This is where the Aaker Brand Equity model becomes useful.

In this article, we would discuss the Aaker brand equity model, its components, its advantages to your brand, and more.

### What is Brand Equity?

Brand equity is the value that culminates into a financial reward for an organization based on customer perception of the brand. For instance, big brands like Apple have enormous brand equity since customers are loyal to these brands, and would choose Apple over other brands despite the price.

Read More – Brand Attitude: What It Is & Why It Matters

This simply means that if Apple made the same products without their brand name on them, it would affect their sales and their profit margin would diminish. This then implies that brand awareness is an important part of brand equity and the level of awareness customers have about a brand is directly proportional to sales, profit, and ultimately commercial value or equity, as these terms are sometimes used interchangeably.

In summary, brand equity is a term that describes the level of influence a brand name has in the mind of the customers. Organizations create brand equity by fostering positive experiences that, make them stand out from the competition and evoke loyalty from their customers. Brand equity is attained by creating brand awareness through campaigns that are tailored to customer values and fulfilling the brand promise.

An organization with positive brand equity can charge a premium for a product, and any product affiliated with or related to the brand can enjoy the same commercial success.

For You: What is Customer Experience Optimization and How To Do It Properly

What is Aaker’s Brand Equity Model?

Aaker’s brand equity model explains brand equity as a mix of brand awareness, loyalty, and quality as perceived by the customer. The Aaker brand model was introduced by David Aaker. a professor from the University of California.

His model believes that brand awareness, customer loyalty, and perceived quality are assets that can help businesses increase the commercial value of their products and services. In his model, he identifies the following as the components of brand equity.

1. Brand Loyalty

This component focuses on the extent to which a company or business can retain its customers in the face of other businesses with similar products. It is evident when a customer grocery shops at a particular store over and over again, this implies that the customer is loyal to that store.

Hence, according to the Aaker model, organizations should focus on growing and maintaining their brand loyalty, in so doing they reduce marketing costs and direct all efforts at ensuring that they do not lose customer trust.

2. Brand Awareness

He defines brand awareness as the level of knowledge or familiarity customers have with a brand. The level of recognition of a brand’s logo message themes and the extent to which customers can associate campaigns, brand voice, products, or services with a brand show or depicts brand awareness.

The Aaker model proposes that organizations that have attained brand awareness can use their visibility to attract more clients. As awareness breeds trust and would cause customers to choose your products over other similar brands.

Read More: What Is Brand Recall, and Why Is It Important?

3. Perceived Quality

The perception in terms of the quality that a brand carries can cause customers to see a brand as reliable and trustworthy. For instance, the cost of an Apple phone is way higher than a Samsung phone. They are both credible brands, however, the perceived quality of Apple products is higher, hence Apple has a price advantage in the market compared to Samsung.

This differentiates Apple distinctly from other competitors in that space.

4. Brand Associations

This component gauges the connections that customers have with a brand, in terms of the information about the brand. The emotions your brand messaging or campaigns evoke are referred to as brand association.

For example, if a customer feels excited, and pumped up, happy after listening to any message associated with your brand, that means your brand has a positive association. This can help increase your commercial value as customers are happy to purchase your brand products or services.

5. Proprietary Assets

Proprietary assets are the final component of brand equity and it refers to intangible assets, owned or possessed by a brand. It includes patents, copyrights, trademarks, and intellectual property rights.

These assets have no monetary value, however, they add to an organization’s credibility, and developing these assets can give companies an edge over their competitors.

### Aaker’s Brand Equity Model vs Keller’s Brand Equity Model

Aaker’s brand equity model and Keller’s brand equity model are part of the various theories that show how marketers can identify, gauge and strengthen a company brand.

Here are some key differences between the two models:

Focus

Aaker’s model focuses on the importance of developing and managing a set of brand assets that are unique to the brand, such as brand personality, brand values, and brand associations. Keller’s model, on the other hand, emphasizes the role of customer perceptions and experiences in shaping brand equity.

Components

Aaker’s model identifies five components of brand equity: brand loyalty, brand awareness, perceived quality, brand associations, and other proprietary brand assets. Keller’s model, on the other hand, identifies four components: brand salience, brand performance, brand imagery, and brand judgments/feelings/resonance.

Structure

Aaker’s model is structured around a set of brand assets that can be developed and managed over time. Keller’s model is based on a set of customer-based brand equity components that reflect the strength of the brand in the minds of customers.

Indicators

Aaker’s model provides a set of indicators for measuring and monitoring brand equity, such as brand awareness, brand loyalty, and brand associations. Keller’s model also provides metrics for measuring brand equity, but these metrics are more focused on customer perceptions and attitudes toward the brand.

Implementation

Aaker’s model is often used by organizations to develop and manage their brand assets, while Keller’s model is mostly used to understand and improve customer perceptions and experiences with the brand.

In summary, while both Aaker’s and Keller’s models provide valuable frameworks for analyzing and managing brand equity, they are different in their focus, components, structure, metrics, and implementation. The choice of which of the models to adopt is based on the specific need and goals of an organization.

### Elements of Brand Identity in the Aaker Model

The Aaker model consists of several elements that an organization can use to define its brand identity. This way. a brand can tailor its product or service to speak to the Aaker brand equity model and they are;

- Brand as a Product

This element of brand identity deals with the product or service. The product quality, specifications, and value to the customer, who it s meant for, and how to use the product. All this set of features highlighted and the value helps to build the strength of the product as a brand.

- Brand as an Organization

The brand as an organization element is the features or attributes of the organization. It may include the organization and the locations it covers. The organizational culture and the value the organization offers. The vision and mission statement of the organization is also included.

- Brand as a Person

This element of brand identity capitalizes on the relationship an organization has with its customers. In other words, if the brand were a person, what would be its traits? It then uses brand messaging and advertising to depict the attributes of its personality and relates to customers in that regard.

- Brand as a Symbol

This is the final element of brand identity in the Aaker model. It involves the symbols associated with the brand and the visual images associated with the brand. The brand logo, themes, colors, and fonts choice are all symbols for the brand that can provide a form of structure for the brand identity.

Advantages Of Aaker Brand Equity Model

Here are some advantages of the Aaker brand equity model

1.) Information Dissemination: The model can help customers have in-depth information about a brand, as detailed information about the brand is shared with customers. This suggests that brand equity can help customers learn, understand and retrieve more information about a brand.

2.) Influence Purchasing: It can also help compel customers to patronize your brand, due to their level of awareness of your brand as depicted in the Aaker brand awareness component.

3.) Customer Satisfaction: The perceived quality of your products as a brand, can impact customer satisfaction positively. As the customers believe that they are getting the best value for their money with your products. Best of all it emphasizes a customer-focused approach, which supports organizations in honing their brand strategies to meet customer needs and preferences.

Explore – Customer Dissatisfaction: The Ultimate Guide

4.) Detailed Framework: The Aaker model provides a complete guide for understanding and using brand equity effectively, as it takes into cognizance all the essential dimensions of brand equity, as well as a comprehensive approach to analyzing and improving brand performance.

5.) Adaptable: The Aaker model is a flexible framework that can be tweaked to suit the requirements of different organizations, hence it can be applied to a broad range of industries and various market conditions.

6.) Measurement and Evaluation: The Aaker model proffers a range of metrics and tools to help organizations gauge and evaluate brand performance.This way they can monitor their progress and identify areas of improvement.

### Disadvantages Of the Aaker Brand Equity Model

1.) Advanced: The Aaker Brand Equity Model is a complex framework that requires a certain level of understanding of marketing and branding concepts to be able to apply effectively. Therefore it may be difficult for newbies in the market space to understand and implement.

2.) Subjectivity: The model relies mainly on the perceptions of customers, which might be a bit technical to gauge and quantify. It can also be affected by individual bias and opinions.

3.) High Investment Cost: Another disadvantage of the Aaker brand equity model is the high financial cost associated with building this model. This is so because advertising involves a significant amount of media presence over a long period, making it an expensive process.

In a nutshell, while the Aaker Brand Equity Model can provide a useful framework for gauging and managing brand equity, however, it would have to be used in addition to other models for a more holistic view of brand performance.

### Conclusion

The Aaker Brand Equity Model is a popular framework developed by David Aaker in 1990. The model defines brand equity or assets as the extent of a customer’s perception of the following components brand awareness, brand loyalty, brand associations, perceived quality, brand association, and proprietary assets.

In other words, the extent to which a customer is aware of a brand and loyal to a brand believes in the quality of a brand, and associates certain emotions with a brand is brand equity.

It states that the level of awareness a customer has about brand equity impacts the financial success of that brand, be it a service or a product. However like any other model, there are advantages and disadvantages, but, it remains a valuable tool for building and sustaining a strong brand.
